title: Cebu Pacific 387
summary: A 30-year-old DC-9 flying from Manila to Cagayan de Oro crashed into Mount Sumagaya during approach. The crew was flying visually in what was believed to be clear weather, but the mountain area was covered by fog. Navigation charts listed the mountain's elevation at 5,000 feet when it actually exceeds 7,300 feet, misleading the crew about terrain clearance. The investigation noted deficiencies in pilot training.
probable_cause: The aircraft struck terrain during visual approach due to erroneous terrain elevation data on navigation charts and low visibility on the mountain slopes.

title: Cavalese cable car disaster
summary: A U.S. Marine Corps EA-6B Prowler struck the cable of an aerial tramway near Cavalese, Italy while flying a low-altitude training mission. The aircraft was flying at 470 knots and 260 feet above ground, well below military regulations and considerably faster than authorized. The plane's right wing severed the cable, causing the cable car to fall and killing twenty people on the ground.
probable_cause: Crew failure to maintain safe altitude and airspeed during low-level training flight. The altimeter was malfunctioning and the crew was unaware of speed restrictions. Navigation maps did not show the cable car cable. An unopened directive forbidding flight below 2000 feet in the area was later found in the cockpit.

title: Formosa Airlines 7623
summary: Formosa Airlines Flight 7623, a Saab 340, crashed into the Taiwan Strait shortly after takeoff at night in instrument meteorological conditions. The aircraft had an unresolved RH Main Bus electrical failure affecting multiple systems including the EFIS display. The flight crew, fatigued after 11+ hours of duty, ignored minimum equipment list requirements and departed anyway. During initial climb, the Captain experienced spatial disorientation and made an aileron input to the right that exacerbated an uncontrolled roll. The aircraft rolled inverted and crashed, killing all 13 aboard.
probable_cause: The crew's decision to operate the aircraft with a known RH Main Bus failure that disabled multiple systems, combined with fatigue and spatial disorientation during night instrument flight, led to loss of control and descent into the Taiwan Strait.

He made a brief aileron input to the right, exacerbating the roll; aircraft rolled to 71 degrees right.
Aircraft rolled inverted with right bank angle 161 degrees and pitch 65 degrees nose down, crashed into Taiwan Strait.

title: Air France 422
summary: A TAME Boeing 727 operating the final leg of Air France Flight 422 crashed into Cerro el Cable near Bogotá less than 2 minutes after takeoff. The first officer, acting as pilot flying, failed to execute the published Girardot 1 departure properly, did not make the required initial turn, and forgot to turn on the transponder. The crew's focus on accelerating to 260 knots resulted in loss of situational awareness and failure to maintain safe altitude, causing impact at 10100 feet.
probable_cause: The crew failed to properly execute the departure procedure and maintain situational awareness during the initial climb.

title: Proteus Airlines 706
summary: Proteus Airlines Flight 706, a Beechcraft 1900D, took off from Lyon on July 30, 1998, bound for Lorient. About seventy minutes into the flight, the crew deviated to Quiberon Bay to show passengers the SS Norway cruise ship. A Cessna 177 from Vannes had taken off for a local flight to Quiberon with its transponder off. During the Beechcraft's descent to 2000 ft while making a 360° turn around the ship, the aircraft collided with the Cessna, and both crashed into the sea.
probable_cause: Collision occurred because the Cessna's transponder was not switched on, rendering it invisible to radar and traffic avoidance systems. The Beechcraft's TCAS had been removed and not approved for operation in France. The cockpit organization and ergonomics during the 360° turn did not allow effective monitoring outside the turn, placing the Cessna in the Beechcraft's blind spot.

title: Swissair 111
summary: Swissair Flight 111, an MD-11 flying from New York to Geneva, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off Peggys Cove, Nova Scotia, on 2 September 1998 after smoke was detected in the cockpit and the crew diverted toward Halifax, killing all 229 aboard. Canada's TSB found that flammable material in the aircraft's structure let the fire spread beyond the crew's control; following the smoke checklist, the crew shut off the cabin bus and recirculation fans, which let the fire reach the cockpit and disable the flight instruments and autopilot before the aircraft struck the water.
probable_cause: The TSB concluded that flammable material used in the aircraft's structure allowed an in-flight fire to spread beyond the flight crew's control, disabling flight instruments and the autopilot and leading to loss of control before impact with the ocean.

factors.evidence: Flammable material used in the aircraft's structure allowed a fire to spread beyond the control of the flight crew, resulting in the crash of the aircraft.
The flight crew detected an odour in the cockpit and determined it to be smoke from the air conditioning system, and smoke became visible four minutes later.

In accordance with the Swissair checklist 'Smoke/fumes of unknown origin', the flight crew shut off power to the cabin using the 'CABIN BUS' switch, which also turned off the recirculating fans, allowing the fire to spread to the cockpit.
In a smoke-filled cockpit and with almost no flight instruments and little to no view outside, Löw may have become spatially disoriented.
Flight 111 struck the ocean at an estimated speed of 345 mph near St. Margarets Bay, killing all 215 passengers and 14 crew members on board.

events.text: At 22:10 ADT while flying over Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, the flight crew detected an odour in the cockpit and determined it was smoke from the air conditioning system.
Four minutes later the odour returned and smoke became visible, prompting the pilots to make a pan-pan call to Moncton Centre and request a diversion.

Following the Swissair 'Smoke/fumes of unknown origin' checklist, the crew shut off power to the cabin using the CABIN BUS switch, which also turned off the recirculating fans and allowed the fire to spread toward the cockpit.
At 22:24:28 the crew reported 'we now must fly manually' as the fire cut power to the autopilot, then declared an emergency ten seconds later in the last transmission received from Flight 111.

In a smoke-filled cockpit with almost no flight instruments, First Officer Löw may have become spatially disoriented, and the aircraft struck the ocean near St. Margarets Bay at an estimated 345 mph at 22:31:18 ADT.

title: PauknAir 4101
summary: PauknAir Flight 4101 departed Málaga at 8:23 AM on September 25, 1998 with 34 passengers and a crew of four. The aircraft descended in instrument meteorological conditions toward Melilla with low visibility due to fog common in the area. The flight crew did not follow the arrival procedure and descended below the minimum safe altitude. At 6:50, the aircraft impacted terrain at 886 feet elevation near Cape Tres Forcas. TAWS warnings had alerted the crew to the terrain but proper procedures were not applied.
probable_cause: Controlled flight into terrain due to non-application of the arrival procedure, inadequate crew coordination, and failure to respond appropriately to GPWS terrain awareness alerts.

title: 1998 Lignes Aériennes Congolaises crash
summary: The aircraft took off from Kindu Airport and began initial climb on a domestic passenger flight to Kinshasa. Three minutes after takeoff, Tutsi rebels fired a missile that struck one of the aircraft's rear engines. The pilot heard firing and reported the hit to air traffic control before reporting the engines were on fire and the plane was becoming uncontrollable. The aircraft crashed in jungle with all 40 to 41 occupants killed. Tutsi rebels admitted shooting down the aircraft, claiming it was carrying military supplies.
